title: The Nichiren schools
hookLine: many schools follow Nichiren's focus on the Lotus Sutra's title

cards: A low, steady sound comes through an apartment door, the same words over and over, like a train on a long track. Nam myoho renge kyo.
Inside, a few neighbors sit side by side, palms together, facing a small wooden cabinet. It sounds like a mantra, and in a way it works like one. But it's something more surprising: a title.
The name of a book, said out loud, with a word of devotion in front. A whole family of Buddhist schools grew up around saying that name.

teach.b: You met Nichiren on day one thousand; today, the family that grew from him. First, the man. Nichiren was a Japanese monk who trained in Tendai, where the Lotus Sutra was already held in honor.
Tradition says he studied widely and came away convinced that the Lotus Sutra was the heart of the Buddha's teaching, and that his country needed to turn back to it.
He said so loudly, and in the stories his followers tell, he paid for it with exile and danger. Second, the big idea. Nichiren taught that the title isn't just a label on the cover.

teach.h: THE TITLE HOLDS THE WHOLE SUTRA.
teach.b: It holds the whole sutra, the way a seed holds a tree. So saying it with faith takes in the entire teaching at once. The practice is called daimoku, the title.
Myoho renge kyo is the Japanese reading of the sutra's name: the wonderful dharma, the lotus flower, the sutra. In front goes namu, or nam, a word of devotion, something like I give myself to.
In Sanskrit the sutra is the Saddharma Pundarika, the lotus of the true dharma. Some communities chant nam, others namu: same title, a different breath. Fourth, what came after.
Nichiren's disciples and their students built many schools and lineages.

Some are temple traditions with priests; some are lay movements that meet in living rooms. They share the sutra and the chant, and they disagree, sometimes sharply, about other things, which the next few days take up.
What they hold in common: a few words, said out loud and meant, can open the Buddha's teaching right inside an ordinary life.

how: Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra, nam myoho renge kyo (or namu myoho renge kyo), often with palms together before a scroll, alone or together in temples and homes.

games.why: he gives them the title. in his teaching, the title holds the whole sutra, so anyone can take it in by chanting it.

practice: Sit upright with your palms together; Nichiren Buddhists face a scroll, and you can face a wall or a window.

Say the title once, slowly, nam myoho renge kyo, or if the words aren't yours to say, hear them once in your mind as a name a whole community holds dear. Then let the sound fade, and rest where it landed in the body.

wordCard.voice: The Nichiren schools. The Buddhist communities that follow the Japanese monk Nichiren in honoring the Lotus Sutra and chanting its title. Today's word.
